chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Hajjaj al-Khashshab, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who was traveling, and when he entered the city, he brought with him two witnesses. When his wife met him at the door, he testified to her divorce. He said: Divorce does not take effect upon her. The meaning in this report is that we interpret it according to what the first report contained, that his divorce takes effect only insofar as she was in her menstruation, because if she had been pure, the divorce would have taken effect as it would have taken effect if he had not been absent at all. It is also possible that the report is specific to one who was absent from his wife during a period of purity, approached her with intercourse, and returned while she was still in that same period of purity; he may not divorce her except after her waiting period (istibra') by one menstruation.
ai.seo_question: When does a returning traveler's divorce take effect according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from al-Isfarayini’s chain to clarify the juristic debate regarding the validity of a husband's divorce upon returning from travel, specifically when he witnesses his wife at the door. The text resolves the ambiguity by interpreting the report as either referring to a wife currently menstruating (where divorce is immediate) or a wife in a state of purity where the husband had intercourse before departure (requiring *istibra'* to confirm non-pregnancy). This highlights the Shia emphasis on contextualizing hadith to reconcile apparent contradictions in marital law.
